# gVisor vs Firecracker for untrusted code

gVisor is an application kernel. It implements a Linux-like interface in Go, a memory-safe language, and runs in userspace. Each sandbox gets its own kernel, so system calls from untrusted code are handled there instead of by the host kernel. The goal is to reduce exposure to host kernel bugs. It ships an OCI runtime, runsc, that works with Docker and Kubernetes. gVisor says it is neither a syscall filter nor a conventional VM. It keeps a process-like resource model and fast startup, but gives no protection against hardware side channels.

Firecracker is a virtual machine monitor built on Linux KVM. Each process runs exactly one microVM with its own guest kernel. The guest sees a minimal device model: VirtIO net and block, serial console, and a keyboard controller. The design document treats all guest vCPU threads as malicious. It adds seccomp filters, cgroups, namespaces, and a jailer that drops privileges. It does not filter guest network traffic, so the host must do that. The NSDI 2020 paper describes it as built for serverless workloads, and it runs AWS Lambda and Fargate.

Trade-off: gVisor offers a lighter, container-native boundary. Firecracker offers a hardware-virtualization boundary and runs a full Linux guest kernel. gVisor's own FAQ says neither approach is inherently more secure.
